First-order drives (A, V) map to a vector field in behavioral space, generating stable attractors representing core needs. Second-order drives (C, G, I) function as scalar fields that modify these attractors' basins, introducing variability and adaptability. Specific appetites (S) encode evolutionary adaptations as fixed point mappings in this system. Failure modes include drive conflict when A + V > 1, leading to oscillatory behavior, and insufficient cognitive modulation when C + G + I < 0.5, resulting in rigid responses. The system's stability depends on the balance between intrinsic motivational forces and extrinsic cognitive regulation.
